In [[complex analysis]], [[functional analysis]] and [[operator theory]], a '''Bergman space''', named after [[Stefan Bergman]], is a [[function space]] of [[holomorphic function]]s in a [[Domain (mathematical analysis)|domain]] ''D'' of the [[complex plane]] that are sufficiently well-behaved at the boundary and also absolutely [[integrable]]. Specifically, for {{math|0 < ''p'' < &infin;}}, the Bergman space {{math|''A''<sup>''p''</sup>(''D'')}} is the space of all holomorphic functions <math>f</math> in ''D'' for which the [[Norm mathematics|''p''-norm]] is finite:

:<math>\|f\|_{A^p(D)} := \left(\int_D |f(x+iy)|^p\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy\right)^{1/p} < \infty.</math>

The quantity <math>\|f\|_{A^p(D)}</math> is called the ''norm'' of the function <math>f</math>; it is a true [[Norm (mathematics)|norm]] if <math>p \geq 1</math>, thus {{math|''A''<sup>''p''</sup>(''D'')}} is the subspace of holomorphic functions of the space [[Lp space|L<sup>''p''</sup>(''D'')]]. The Bergman spaces are [[Banach space]]s for <math>0 < p < \infty</math>, which is a consequence of the following estimate that is valid on [[compact space|compact]] subsets ''K'' of ''D'':<math display="block">\sup_{z\in K} |f(z)| \leq C_K \|f\|_{L^p(D)}.</math>Convergence of a sequence of holomorphic functions in {{math|''L''<sup>''p''</sup>(''D'')}} thus implies [[compact convergence]], and so the limit function is also holomorphic.

If {{math|''p'' {{=}} 2}}, then {{math|''A''<sup>''p''</sup>(''D'')}} is a [[reproducing kernel Hilbert space]], whose kernel is given by the [[Bergman kernel]].

==Special cases and generalisations==

If the domain {{math|''D''}} is [[Bounded set (topological vector space)|bounded]], then the norm is often given by:

:<math>\|f\|_{A^p(D)} := \left(\int_D |f(z)|^p\,dA\right)^{1/p} \; \; \; \; \; (f \in A^p(D)),</math>

where <math>A</math> is a normalised [[Lebesgue measure]] of the complex plane, i.e. {{math|''dA'' {{=}} ''dz''/Area(''D'')}}. Alternatively {{math|''dA'' {{=}} ''dz''/''π''}} is used, regardless of the area of {{math|''D''}}.
The Bergman space is usually defined on the open [[unit disk]] <math>\mathbb{D}</math> of the complex plane, in which case <math>A^p(\mathbb{D}):=A^p</math>. If <math>p=2</math>, given an element <math>f(z)= \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n z^n \in A^2</math>, we have

:<math>\|f\|^2_{A^2} := \frac{1}{\pi} \int_\mathbb{D} |f(z)|^2 \, dz = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{|a_n|^2}{n+1},</math>

that is, {{math|''A''<sup>2</sup>}} is isometrically isomorphic to the weighted [[Sequence space#.E2.84.93p spaces|''ℓ''<sup>''p''</sup>(1/(''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1)) space]].<ref name="Duren"/> In particular, not only are the [[polynomial]]s [[dense subset|dense]] in {{math|''A''<sup>2</sup>}}, but every function <math>f \in A^2</math> can be uniformly approximated by radial dilations of functions <math>g</math> holomorphic on a disk <math>D_R(0)</math>, where <math>R > 1</math> and the radial dilation of a function is defined by <math>g_r(z) := g(rz)</math> for <math>0 < r < 1</math>.

Similarly, if {{math|''D'' {{=}} <math>\mathbb{C}</math><sub>+</sub>}}, the right (or the upper) complex half-plane, then:

:<math>\|F\|^2_{A^2(\mathbb{C}_+)} := \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{\mathbb{C}_+} |F(z)|^2 \, dz = \int_0^\infty |f(t)|^2\frac{dt}{t},</math>

where <math>F(z)= \int_0^\infty f(t)e^{-tz} \, dt</math>, that is, <math>A^2(\mathbb{C}_+)</math> is isometrically isomorphic to the weighted [[Lp space|''L''<sup>''p''</sup><sub>1/''t''</sub> (0,∞) space]] (via the [[Laplace transform]]).<ref name="Duren1969" /><ref name="Jacob" />

The weighted Bergman space {{math|''A''<sup>''p''</sup>(''D'')}} is defined in an analogous way,<ref name="Duren"/> i.e.,

:<math>\|f\|_{A^p_w (D)} := \left( \int_D |f(x+iy)|^2 \, w(x+iy) \, dx \, dy \right)^{1/p}, </math>

provided that {{math|''w'' : ''D'' → [0, &infin;)}} is chosen in such way, that <math>A^p_w(D)</math> is a [[Banach space]] (or a [[Hilbert space]], if {{math|''p'' {{=}} 2}}). In case where <math> D= \mathbb{D}</math>, by a weighted Bergman space <math>A^p_\alpha</math><ref name="Cowen"/> we mean the space of all analytic functions {{math|''f''}} such that:

:<math> \|f\|_{A^p_\alpha} := \left( (\alpha+1)\int_\mathbb{D} |f(z)|^p \, (1-|z|^2)^\alpha dA(z) \right)^{1/p} < \infty, </math>

and similarly on the right half-plane (i.e., <math>A^p_\alpha(\mathbb{C}_+)</math>) we have:<ref name="Elliott"/>

:<math> \|f\|_{A^p_\alpha(\mathbb{C}_+)} := \left( \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}_+} |f(x+iy)|^p x^\alpha \, dx \, dy \right)^{1/p}, </math>

and this space is isometrically isomorphic, via the Laplace transform, to the space <math>L^2(\mathbb{R}_+, \, d\mu_\alpha)</math>,<ref name="Duren2007"/><ref name="Gallardo"/> where:

:<math>d\mu_\alpha := \frac{\Gamma(\alpha+1)}{2^\alpha t^{\alpha+1}} \, dt.</math>

Here {{math|&Gamma;}} denotes the [[Gamma function]].

Further generalisations are sometimes considered, for example <math>A^2_\nu</math> denotes a weighted Bergman space (often called a Zen space<ref name="Jacob"/>) with respect to a translation-invariant positive regular [[Borel measure]] <math>\nu</math> on the closed right complex half-plane <math>\overline{\mathbb{C}_+}</math>, that is:

:<math>A^p_\nu := \left\{ f : \mathbb{C}_+ \longrightarrow \mathbb{C} \text{ analytic} \; : \; \|f\|_{A^p_\nu} := \left( \sup_{\varepsilon>0} \int_{\overline{\mathbb{C}_+}} |f(z+\varepsilon)|^p \, d\nu(z) \right)^{1/p} < \infty \right\}. </math>
It is possible to generalise <math>A^2</math> to the (weighted) Bergman space of vector-valued functions,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Aleman |first=Alexandru |last2=Constantin |first2=Olivia |date=2004 |title=Hankel operators on Bergman spaces and similarity to contractions |url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8160019 |journal=International Mathematics Research Notices |volume=2004 |issue=35 |pages=1785–1801 |doi=10.1155/S1073792804140105 |issn=1687-0247 |doi-access =<!-- not free-->}}</ref> defined by<math display="block">A^{2}_\alpha(\mathbb{D}; \mathcal{H}) := \left\{\, f \colon \, \mathbb{D} \to \mathcal{H} \; | \;f \text{ analytic and } \|f\|_{2, \alpha} < +\infty  \right\},</math>and the norm on this space is given as<math display="block">\|f\|_{2, \alpha} = \left(\int_{\mathbb{D}} \|f(z)\|_{\mathcal{H}}^2d\mu_\alpha(z)\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}.</math>The measure <math>\mu_\alpha</math> is the same as the previous measure on the weighted Bergman space over the unit disk, <math>\mathcal{H}</math> is a Hilbert space. In this case, the space is a Banach space for <math>0 < p \leq \infty</math> and a (reproducing kernel) Hilbert space when <math>p=2</math>.

==Reproducing kernels==
{{main|Bergman kernel}}
The reproducing kernel <math>k_z^{A^2}</math> of {{math|''A''<sup>2</sup>}} at point <math>z \in \mathbb{D}</math> is given by:<ref name="Duren"/>

:<math> k_z^{A^2}(\zeta)=\frac{1}{(1-\overline{z}\zeta)^2} \; \; \; \; \; (\zeta \in \mathbb{D}),</math>

and similarly, for <math>A^2(\mathbb{C}_+)</math> we have:<ref name="Elliott"/>

:<math> k_z^{A^2(\mathbb{C}_+)}(\zeta)=\frac{1}{(\overline{z}+\zeta)^2} \; \; \; \; \; (\zeta \in \mathbb{C}_+),</math>

In general, if <math>\varphi</math> maps a domain <math>\Omega</math> conformally onto a domain <math>D</math>, then:<ref name="Duren"/>

:<math>k^{A^2(\Omega)}_z (\zeta) = k^{\mathcal{A}^2(D)}_{\varphi(z)}(\varphi(\zeta)) \, \overline{\varphi'(z)}\varphi'(\zeta) \; \; \; \; \; (z, \zeta \in \Omega).</math>

In weighted case we have:<ref name="Cowen"/>

:<math>k_z^{A^2_\alpha} (\zeta) = \frac{\alpha+1}{(1-\overline{z}\zeta)^{\alpha+2}} \; \; \; \; \; (z, \zeta \in \mathbb{D}),</math>

and:<ref name="Elliott"/>

:<math>k_z^{A^2_\alpha(\mathbb{C}_+)} (\zeta) = \frac{2^\alpha(\alpha+1)}{(\overline{z}+\zeta)^{\alpha+2}} \; \; \; \; \; (z, \zeta \in \mathbb{C}_+).</math>
In any reproducing kernel Bergman space, functions obey a certain property. It is called the '''reproducing property.''' This is expressed as a formula as follows: For any function <math>f \in A^2</math> (respectively other Bergman spaces that are RKHS), it is true that<math display="block">f(z) = \langle f, k_z^{A^2} \rangle_{2} = \int_{\mathbb{D}} \frac{f(\zeta)}{(1-z\overline{\zeta})^2}dA.</math>
